A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 4D Gaussian scene-editing work, with matching core sections, equations, tables and figures. The supplied material is readable. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Supplementary Material Sections 7–8 and Figures 9–11.

before.justification: v1 reports original DyNeRF editing results, quantitative quality and timing comparisons in Tables 1–2, and ablation results with a 50-participant preference study in Figure 8.

after.justification: v2 reports revised quantitative editing results, retains the timing and user-study outcomes, and adds original qualitative evaluations on Technicolor, DyCheck and HyperNeRF, plus a viewpoint-consistency evaluation.

M1.justification: The main two-stage multiview method remains intact. Section 7.1 adds a monocular operating mode that skips Stage 1 and uses only Stage 2 because multiview supervision is unavailable. This adaptation reuses the SDS-only approach already examined as the Fully SDS ablation in v1; it introduces no new architecture or loss.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates DyNeRF multiview scenes. v2 adds Technicolor's Painter and Train scenes and monocular evaluations on DyCheck's mochi-high-five and HyperNeRF's Interp chickchicken scenes. These substantially broaden the represented environments and input-capture conditions beyond the original multiview setting.

E2.justification: Instruct 4D-to-4D remains the external comparator in Table 1 and the qualitative comparisons. Its application to Technicolor and DyCheck extends the same comparator to new coverage. The four variants compared in Figure 8 also remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes the reported average refinement budget from 500 to 800 iterations and text guidance from 10.5 to 8.5–10.5. Section 5.2 replaces v1's explicit pre-refinement restriction for PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS with an edited-scene evaluation description and discusses refinement's effect on those metrics. v2 also reports 50-frame trimming for baseline comparisons, although its precise scope is unclear, and adds novel-camera-pose testing.

E4.justification: Section 7.2 and Figure 11 add a qualitative spatial-consistency check by rendering edited DyNeRF scenes from different camera poses. The existing temporal-refinement demonstration, component ablations and 50-participant preference study are retained with the same evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The preference study retains 50 participants and the same percentage-based reporting practice; its pie-chart percentages are unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces all proposed-method scores: average PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/CLIP change from 27.22/0.856/0.250/0.256 to 19.25/0.783/0.303/0.249. Baseline values stay fixed, and v2 no longer leads every metric, including average PSNR. These are revised results under changed reported settings, not an established same-setting performance decline. Figures 6 and 9–11 add qualitative results; Table 2 retains 40 minutes on one GPU versus two hours on two GPUs.

T1.justification: The rendering expression preceding Equation 1 removes an additional deformation term from an already deformed Gaussian representation. Given Section 3's definition, this corrects a redundant deformation addition. The SDS and guidance equations and the remaining mathematical definitions are unchanged; neither version contains new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims about static-component editing, Coherent-IP2P refinement and reducing editing time by more than half. The conclusion modestly narrows its performance claim from superiority in visual metrics to superior visual quality, consistent with v2's acknowledgment of weaker PSNR/SSIM in some cases.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 replaces blanket metric superiority with an explanation of pixel-accuracy versus perceptual-quality tradeoffs during refinement. Section 7.1 adds qualified discussion of monocular applicability and dependence on reconstruction/SDS quality. The main limitations remain, but v2 drops v1's specific attribution of deformation-field refinement failures to Coherent-IP2P not being a video diffusion model.

D1.justification: New Section 8 supplies exact editing instructions for Table 1 and Figures 5–6, expanding on v1's abbreviated style labels. Section 5.1 revises the disclosed guidance scale and refinement budget. The Stage 1 iteration range and NVIDIA A40 hardware remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds dataset references for DyCheck, HyperNeRF and Technicolor. The related-work categories, positioning against Instruct 4D-to-4D and claimed novelty of efficient 4DGS-based editing remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites paragraphs across the introduction, related work, method explanations, results, ablations and conclusion, including passages with unchanged scientific meaning. It introduces the Instruct-4DGS name throughout, renames Section 6 to Conclusion and Limitations, and adds supplementary Sections 7–8. The main section order remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 6 expands from a single-column comparison to a full-width display covering four scenes with additional comparison panels. v2 adds Figures 9–11, relocates the retained Figures 7–8, revises captions and reorders Table 1's instruction blocks. These substantially expand and reorganize the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the paper through broader qualitative evaluation, the viewpoint-consistency check and exact editing prompts. Its revised discussion acknowledges pixel-metric weaknesses instead of claiming universal metric superiority, improving the calibration of its conclusions. These are useful but bounded gains: the added domains receive qualitative evaluation, and ambiguity in the revised evaluation description limits interpretation of Table 1's changes.
